name: Unity Cable System

profile.address: 3721, 148th Street Southwest, Lynnwood, Snohomish County, Washington, 98087
profile.reading:
The Norma Beach Cable Landing Station sits on Puget Sound in Lynnwood, Washington, near Picnic Point in Snohomish County, at the shoreline point where a transoceanic fiber optic cable comes ashore from the Pacific. Public evidence, including the cable's own documented landing points, points to this building serving the Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, a subsea network built and operated by GCI, formerly General Communication, Inc., Alaska's largest telecommunications provider. The Alaska United system's AU-East segment was laid in the second half of 1999 at an initial cost of roughly 120 million dollars, one of two major undersea cable projects that year aimed at bringing modern high speed connectivity to Alaska. It replaced the earlier North Pacific Cable, which was retired in 2004. AU-East links Anchorage and Lena Point near Juneau to the Lower 48 at Norma Beach, while a separate AU-West segment lands at Seward, Alaska and Warrenton, Oregon. As of the most recent public reporting located, both segments carry OC-192 capacity, roughly 10 gigabits per second, though undersea cable capacity is frequently upgraded through equipment changes that are not always announced publicly.

Some published references associate this address with an operator called Unity Cable System, but that attribution does not match the physical and historical evidence. Unity is a real and well documented transpacific cable, built by a consortium including Google, Bharti Airtel, Global Transit, KDDI, Pacnet and SingTel and completed in 2010, but its United States landing point is in Redondo Beach, California, several hundred miles south of Puget Sound and on an entirely different approach route from Asia. Nothing in the public record ties a Unity Cable System landing station to Lynnwood, Washington, while GCI's own network materials and the documented history of the Alaska United system point consistently to Norma Beach as an Alaska United landing site. The Unity Cable System name appears to be a misattribution for this address, and readers should not rely on it.

Cable landing stations like this one are typically unstaffed or lightly staffed technical buildings housing optical transmission equipment, power backup, and the interconnection point where a submarine cable's signal is handed off to terrestrial fiber networks. GCI describes having invested more than 5 billion dollars in its network overall, including infrastructure serving remote regions of Alaska, though the company does not publish building specific details such as square footage or backup power capacity for this station. That is typical of landing stations generally, which are usually treated as sensitive infrastructure with minimal public description beyond their general location and the cable system they serve.

profile.research_note:
Operator/facility mismatch: this facility (Norma Beach Cable Landing Station, Lynnwood WA) actually belongs to the Alaska United cable system operated by GCI, not the Unity cable system, whose real US landing point is Redondo Beach, CA. Flagged for a facility-level operator correction to GCI rather than reassigned now, per no-delete policy.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This registry row is attributed to Unity Cable System, which corresponds to a real, well documented trans Pacific submarine fiber optic cable, completed in 2010 by a consortium including Google, Bharti Airtel, Global Transit, KDDI, Pacnet, and SingTel, connecting Chikura, Japan to Redondo Beach, California. However, the facility actually linked to this record is the Norma Beach Cable Landing Station near Lynnwood, Washington, on Puget Sound, which is not part of the Unity system at all. Norma Beach is instead the Washington State landing point for the Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, a separate submarine cable owned and operated by GCI, formerly General Communication Inc, the Alaska based telecommunications company, connecting Anchorage and Juneau, Alaska to the Pacific Northwest. The Unity cable actual US landing point is in Redondo Beach, California, several hundred miles south, an entirely different cable system and operator. This appears to be a genuine name to facility mismatch in the underlying registry data rather than an obscure or hard to find entity. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading: This operator record is named Unity Cable System, which corresponds to a real, well documented trans Pacific submarine fiber optic cable, completed in 2010 by a consortium including Google, Bharti Airtel, Global Transit, KDDI, Pacnet, and SingTel, connecting Chikura, Japan to Redondo Beach, California. However, the single facility linked to this operator record in the registry is the Norma Beach Cable Landing Station near Lynnwood, Washington, on Puget Sound, which is not part of the Unity system at all. Norma Beach is instead the Washington State landing point for the Alaska United Fiber Optic Cable System, a separate submarine cable owned and operated by GCI, formerly General Communication Inc, the Alaska based telecommunications company, connecting Anchorage and Juneau, Alaska to the Pacific Northwest. The Unity cable's actual US landing point is in Redondo Beach, California, several hundred miles south, an entirely different cable system and operator. This appears to be a genuine name to facility mismatch in the underlying registry data, similar in kind to other mismatches identified during this research, rather than a case where Unity Cable System is simply an obscure or hard to find entity. Because assigning capacity or infrastructure detail to Unity Cable System based on a facility that actually belongs to a different cable system and a different operator would misrepresent both companies, this record is marked exhausted with no operator type assigned, and the facility record should be corrected during the facility level research phase to reflect its actual operator, GCI, and its actual cable system, Alaska United.
